extracted.intended_audience: educated readers of essays on politics, philosophy, literature, and law (general public, lawyers, and literary students)
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of essay-style aphorisms and practical prescriptions covering literary criticism, philosophical method, legal/advocate ethics, and political conduct. The content mixes prescriptive judgments about good practice with examples and commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocate ethical limits and duties
rubrics_metrics.description: An advocate has a right and bounden duty to do everything which his client might honestly do, and to do it with all the effect which skill, talent, or knowledge may produce; but he has no right nor duty to do what his client in foro conscientiae has no right to do for himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit prohibition example: not to put in evidence a forged deed or will, knowing it to be forged. The author allows a certain latitude in examining witnesses (described as 'cudgel-playing') as a necessary mean toward eliciting truth; advocates should aim to equalize knowledge between crown and prisoner or plaintiff and defendant. To counteract the narrowing effects of legal practice, advocates are advised to study metaphysics (or metaphysics of theology) in leisure to ennoble intellect and foster truth-seeking rather than partisanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zealous representation within honest bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocates should zealously represent their clients within the bounds of honesty and law, employing all legitimate skill and knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While confounding witnesses by skilful cross-examination is not condemned strictly, outright fraudulent or conscience-violating acts are forbidden. The necessities of society may justify some practical latitude in courtroom tactics, but moral limits remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocates should cultivate broad intellectual studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal practice sharpens but narrows intellectual faculties; advocates should pursue studies (e.g., metaphysics) that call forth higher powers and centre wishes in truth-alone investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphysical study is recommended to balance the sharpening/narrowing effect of legal work and to develop powers of distinction and truth-seeking beyond partisan advocacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical system should unify partial truths
rubrics_metrics.description: A sound philosophical system attempts to reduce all knowledges into harmony, showing what is true in each system and explaining how partial truths became errors by being half-truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author describes the method: acknowledge each system's truth, 'lift up that system to a higher point of view' so former positions appear as parts of a broader whole. Example aims include connecting natural history with political history and making history scientific while making science historical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between keenness and subtlety
rubrics_metrics.description: Subtlety and keenness are distinct intellectual qualities: keenness is like a point (ability to split a hair), subtlety is like an edge (ability to distinguish differences that appear identical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Few men of genius are keen, but almost every man of genius is subtle. Subtlety is valued for showing that two apparently identical things are in fact different; mere hair-splitting is not subtlety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral principles must be grounded in reason and duty, not mere pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest-happiness (pleasure) principle is inadequate as a governing motive because happiness is a natural instinct and varies among individuals; instead, one needs a standard of reason and duty 'imperative upon our merely pleasurable sensations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique addresses utilitarian formulations: defining 'happiness' is subjective (e.g., savage vs. civilized notions). To avoid sacrificing real good to particular views, moral action must aim at goods that reason, common to all, pronounces as good for all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate truths from maxims
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the essential difference between reason and understanding, between a principle/truth perceived by intuitive reason and a maxim generalized from experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maxims (generalized conclusions from repeated experience) are provisional and may be overturned by counterexamples; eternal truths (e.g., geometric truths) are perceived immediately by reason and are independent of experience. The author gives examples (moss roses, triangles) to illustrate the distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love of truth must accompany love of the good
rubrics_metrics.description: Loving the good for the good's sake without loving the truth for the truth's sake can lead to persecution and inquisitorial cruelty; only those who love both sincerely see their ultimate identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical observation: in countries professing Romish religion, the end-justifies-means mentality (love of good without truth-love) produced inquisitorial cruelty. Counsel to value truth to prevent the persecution of truth under the guise of doing good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political action: appeal to duty and universal moral truths
rubrics_metrics.description: Statesmen should take their stand upon duty and appeal to all men as men—to the Good and the True which exist for all—rather than addressing measures solely to individual interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The demagogues appeal broadly to abstract phrases (e.g., 'Rights of Man') which sweep general passions; good political leadership should appeal to universal moral principles and sound duty to avoid volatile popular convulsions. The author laments lack of leaders who will sound the word 'Duty.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Statesmanship: avoid manipulating popular passions and preserve deliberation
rubrics_metrics.description: Ministers should not excite passions or play upon the ignorance of the numerical majority to carry fundamental changes; they must preserve freedom and utility of discussion by competent deliberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific criticisms of Reform Bill conduct: (1) do not preclude competent discussion by stoking popular passions and appealing to sheer numbers regardless of competence; (2) do not make the sovereign the instrument of such manipulations. Maintain representation of interests and honest explanation of anomalies rather than vilification and theatrical appeals to the mob.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural honor in constitutional change (peers' conduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: If abolition of hereditary peerage is the genuine will of the nation, the proper course is for the king and deputies to form a constituent assembly to decree the change; peers should, as men of honour, refuse peerages created de novo for life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peers ought to defend their constitutional role if convinced of its importance; but if the nation truly demands abolition, peers should yield as private citizens to the constituted process rather than participate in a revolutionary usurpation. Advice includes printing balanced arguments and seeking fresh instructions if deputies claim to be bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for poetic quality: purity of diction and study of predecessors
rubrics_metrics.description: Good poetry exhibits pure diction (language that has a longstanding social locus) and benefits from diligent improvement of natural talent and study of elder poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Daniel's diction is 'pre-eminently pure' and akin to forms used by distinguished modern writers; Drayton shows instances of sublimity. The youth entering poetry without respect for elder poets is unlikely to achieve durable work; industrious improvement and gratitude toward predecessors are counselled.
